By comprehensively understanding the root causes of pain points within the customer or employee journey, project teams are equipped to prioritize and design targeted improvements that directly address these issues. Guided by the scope and objectives detailed in the Lean-Agile Project Charter, this analysis ensures that pain points are addressed according to their impact and the feasibility of solutions within planned releases. This strategic approach prevents the inefficiency of trying to tackle all improvement opportunities simultaneously, instead enabling focused enhancements in manageable phases. Additionally, the analysis fosters a deeper understanding of customer or employee behaviors, values, and expectations, which helps unify departments around the common goal of improving the overall experience. Ultimately, Customer Journey Pain Points Analysis sets the groundwork for developing a future state valuestream and journey that systematically resolves identified issues, ensuring alignment with the organization's strategic objectives and promoting a coherent and effective transformation journey. How to do Journey Mapping? Journey Mapping: Frontstage – How to Frame the journey Journey maps can illustrate either existing experiences (current-state journey maps) or new experiences that are planned but do not yet exist (future- state journey maps). Before beginning Journey Mapping, it is important to define the specific journey or journeys that you will be focusing on and the specific customer perspective that you will be adopting. This involves agreeing the boundaries of the chosen journey and the personas that will be used. Define the journey phases Agree the customer journey phases and sub-phases with key stakeholders to provide the structure of the map. These represent the high-level sections of an experience, such as “inspiration, planning, booking, experience, sharing” for a holiday. These stages define the scale of your visualised experience. ntation method to provide useful insights for design. BEHAVIOURAL Behavioural segmentation involves segmenting customers based on the way they interact with a brand. Common variables include usage (i.e. purchase frequency), exhibited behaviour and habits (i.e. adding product to cart but not checking out), and product / service preferences. This approach can be very granular, e.g. tracking customers’ online interactions, and is based on proven consumer habits and practices. It is particularly helpful for targeting marketing interventions to boost conversion. However, while consumer behaviour can be tracked, it is not always easy to pinpoint the motivations behind those behaviours, as they can vary greatly from person to person. Also, behavioural segmentation is often based on complex data constructs that are not always easy to understand. ATTITUDINAL Attitudinal (or psychographic) segmentation takes into account the psychological aspects of consumer behaviour by dividing markets according to lifestyle, personality traits, values, opinions, and interests of consumers.
